story_name: Stormcaller: The Eye of the Sky
story_overview: A boy named Raiden discovers he can call lightning with his voice. He has been hiding this ability in a world that fears weather-mages after a great storm destroyed a kingdom a generation ago. When a drought begins killing crops and rivers dry up, Raiden must reveal himself and call a storm that will save the land — knowing it will also reveal what he is to people who may never forgive him.

speech: He did not ask the storm for permission. He never did. That was, depending on who you asked, either his greatest flaw or his most important gift.
The earth was dying. You could see it in the cracks. You could feel it in the air. The sky had forgotten how to cry, and the land was paying the price.
Raiden walked home through fields that should have been gold. They were brown instead. Brown and brittle and begging for something that would not come.
He had a secret in his chest. It felt like thunder waiting to break. He had held it inside for so long he had forgotten what silence felt like.
That night, he stood at his window. The sky was empty. But somewhere deep in his bones, he felt clouds gathering. They were not in the sky yet. They were in him.

speech: He whispered to the sky. Not words. Something older than words. A sound that came from the back of his throat and the bottom of his lungs and somewhere even deeper than that.
The sky did not answer. It never did. But something in his chest answered. Something that had been sleeping since the day he was born.
Lightning jumped from his fingers. Just a flicker. Just a taste. The ground smoked where it hit. For one second, the field was blue. Then darkness again.
He looked at his hands. They were just hands. They had held tools and food and his mother's face. They had also just held lightning.
He went home before anyone saw. The secret was still safe. But the secret was getting heavier. Secrets do that when you carry them alone.

speech: The well had given water for three hundred years. That morning, it gave dust. The bucket came up empty. So did the next one. And the next.
The women did not cry. They had used up their tears last month. Now they just stood there, holding buckets, waiting for a miracle that was late.
A child tugged on Raiden's sleeve. 'When will it rain?' The boy did not have an answer. But his bones did. His bones knew exactly when.
He looked at the sky. Still white. Still empty. Still cruel. And he felt the storm inside him pressing against his ribs like a caged animal.
He walked away from the well. He could feel their eyes on his back. They did not know what he was. If they knew, they would be afraid. And they would be right.

speech: His mother fell like a dry leaf. No sound. No warning. Just the earth rising up to meet her and her son's arms barely fast enough to catch her.
He held her. She was light. Too light. The drought had been eating her from the inside, and he had been too afraid to notice.
Her lips moved. No sound came out. But he knew what she was trying to say. 'It's okay. It's not your fault.' But it was. It was.
He looked up at the sky. The white, empty, mocking sky. And for the first time in his life, he did not try to hold the storm back.
He opened his mouth. And the sound that came out was not a word. It was a thunderclap. It was a century of silence breaking all at once.

speech: He screamed. And the sky answered. Not because it wanted to. Because it had no choice. His voice was not a request. It was a command.
Lightning poured from his mouth like he had been swallowing storms his whole life and finally decided to spit them back out.
The clouds came from nowhere. They boiled up from the horizon like an army finally arriving after a very long march. The wind picked up. The temperature dropped.
Raiden stood in the middle of the field with his arms raised. He was on fire with electricity. He was also crying. No one could see the tears through the rain that had not started yet.
The village heard the thunder. They came to their doors. They looked at the sky. And then they looked at the boy standing in the field with lightning in his hands. And they were afraid.

speech: The village came out to watch. Some of them held tools that could become weapons. Some of them held children. Some of them just held their breath.
An old man who remembered the last weather-mage squinted at Raiden. 'He has her eyes,' he said. No one asked who 'her' was. They already knew.
A child pointed. 'He's making it rain.' The sky was still dry. But the child was not wrong. The rain was coming. You could feel it in the air now.
A man with a pitchfork stepped forward. Another man grabbed his arm. 'Wait,' he said. 'Let him finish. We can be afraid after the rain.'
Raiden's mother opened her eyes. She saw her son standing in a field of lightning. She did not look afraid. She looked like she had always known.

speech: The first drop hit the earth like a whisper. The second was louder. By the third, the sky was shouting.
The village did not run for cover. They had been running from the sun for months. They stood in the rain and let it wash them clean.
An old woman opened her mouth and let the rain fall on her tongue. She had forgotten what water tasted like. Now she would never forget again.
Children splashed in puddles that had not existed five minutes ago. Their laughter was louder than the thunder. Almost.
Raiden stood alone in the field. The lightning had stopped. The storm was just a storm now. He lowered his arms. And then he felt it — his mother's arms around him from behind.

speech: The rain lasted three days. When it stopped, the world was different. The cracks in the earth had closed. The cracks in the village were still there. But they were smaller.
Raiden walked through the fields. Green was coming back. Small green shoots pushing through mud that used to be dust. Life is stubborn that way.
A farmer nodded at him. Not a bow. Not a accusation. Just a nod. The kind of nod you give someone who saved your life when you were not looking.
The river was running again. Children splashed in it. Their parents did not tell them to come out. Some things are more important than being dry.

Raiden sat on a hill with his mother. Neither of them spoke. The storm was over. The secret was out. And for the first time in his life, he did not have to hide. That, he decided, was almost as good as rain.
